result: Goal set: read the delivered documents in order and answer later questions about the retellings only, ignoring unrelated documents. This will now anchor every prompt.
OK

Narrator Vira Toland, a Hessel Bottom patron's daughter recalls how the 1919 "water in the milk" accusation against station tester Ansel Keddie (her mother's cousin by marriage into the Vose family) fractured her family's community, only later revealed as Keddie skimming cream, and left lasting shame decades on.
This report is from 1966 (recommending a levy of six mills on the dollar for 1967) and contains no information about a 1908 levy.

Narrator Effie Loomis, the Association's secretary 1901–1940, gives an institutional/documentary history of the Larrow Valley Creamery, tracing Article VII's "station test governs" rule to the 1925 arbitration that paid Ostrey Hollow patrons $3,800 while "finding no cause," and flags a never-discussed 1923 condemned measures crate as the record's key silence.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Narrator Ansel Keddie, the ousted station tester himself, defends his testing procedure in an 1925 board statement and unsent letter detailing decades of meticulous records, the unexplained 1911 measure anomaly, and the family rift with brother-in-law Emmet Brant after the 1919 circular—insisting he never took cream and cannot explain the persistent low test figures.
The wholesale order Elias Norcross placed with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 totaled $59.65.

Narrator Ivy Keddie, Ansel Keddie's granddaughter, presenting to the Ordell County Historical Society in 1959, uses forensic measurement of the condemned pipettes found in the storage crate to prove the station's low tests were caused by consistently short-delivering glassware (95% of the calibrated mark)—not cream theft or watered milk—exonerating her grandfather decades after his death.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Narrator Wilbur Teague, the Association's bookkeeper 1905–1945, recounts how his own "station gain" ledger entries showed a steady 5¼% surplus between credited and actual butterfat every year, which he suspected (and told manager Selby Vose in 1916, but was rebuffed) pointed to cream theft rather than any innocent explanation, testimony he stood by at the 1925 hearing.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for the petty theft of dress goods.

Narrator Merle Strawn, the retired state dairy inspector, presents his terse year-by-year circuit-book log of Ostrey Hollow inspections from 1907–1936, documenting scales always true and no added water found, but crucially recording that on 12 June 1923 he ran the station's pipettes against a new burette, found they would not deliver their mark, and condemned the whole crate—with tests improving thereafter.
Lemma 2.1 is named "Interleaving."

Narrator Halbert Nym, curator of the Ordell County Historical Rooms, presents a 1972 catalogue of 16 accessioned artifacts (pipette crate, ledgers, bulletins, letters) documenting the Ostrey Hollow case—notably mislabeling Item 3 as "kept by E. Brant" (though signed A. Keddie) and Item 4 as "kept by A. Keddie" (though its provenance traces through the Brant family), a labeling swap worth flagging.
Mr. Ansgar Krell remained at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks.

Narrator Selby Vose, the Association's manager, in his 1926 annual address defends the 1925 settlement and insists the real cause of Ostrey Hollow's low tests was patrons watering milk that "stopped when the Association began looking," dismissing the condemned testing apparatus (which he dates to 12 July 1923, a date conflicting with inspector Strawn's 12 June record) as mere routine wear-and-tear housekeeping.
Error code `SKF-2201` (HTTP 400) is returned when a sailings query span exceeds 14 days.

r09 — Narrator Roy Brant (Emmet Brant's son), recounting his father's weigh-book at Hessel Bottom: their own scale weights always matched the station's, confirming no cans were shorted, while the persistent ~0.17-point test gap (unaffected by season, matching the 1911 broken-measure anomaly) pointed to the station's testing apparatus rather than weighing or watering as the true culprit.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for Mrs. Content Averill's confinement (delivery with forceps) on January 3, 1906.

r10 — Narrator Rosalie Cudd, Alder Corners cheesemaker, replying to Ivy Keddie's 1958 inquiry: her father's independent cheese-factory tests on the same four Hessel Bottom farmers' summer milk (1915–1930) consistently ran ~3.80, refuting the "wet hay" and watering theories and corroborating that the Ostrey Hollow station's own readings were the anomaly.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance.

r11 — Narrator Leland Vaught, dairy-husbandry professor, writing the introduction/method section of Bulletin 471 (1958): explains how a short-delivering pipette produces a proportional, invisible test error and uses the 1911 nine-week swap as proof — though this account's own figures (five dozen pipettes, mean delivery 16.27 c.c., ratio 0.9244, 118,000 lb shortfall) conflict with the "16.72 c.c./95%/76,000 lb" figures given in every other retelling, including its own closing paragraph quoted verbatim from Bulletin 471.
The color named in the third paragraph is vermilion (Bettine Rausch's apron).

r12 — Narrator Dell Rundle, Larrow Green schoolteacher, jubilee pamphlet (1939, reprinted 1959) giving the valley's folk history of the Association and the Ostrey Hollow "stolen cream" quarrel, then retracting the theft theory in a press-note after seeing the ledger's "station gain" entry — though her figures (Article VII dated 1891, July 12 1923 condemnation, 44 million lbs intake, $19,600 loss, "eleven pipettes" recovered) diverge from several other accounts.
Message No. 219, "FATHER VERY LOW COME AT ONCE," was 6 words.

r13 — Narrator Alonzo Frick, arbitration chairman, 1946 bar-association reflection on the 1925 Ostrey Hollow hearing: recounts the three competing (unproven) theories aired at the arbitration — watering (Vose), cream theft (Teague's insinuation), and bad hay — plus Keddie's private aside blaming the patrons, and gives figures (3.16 average, 67,000 lb claimed loss, four exhibits) that diverge from several other retellings.
The locksmith's dog is named Buckley.

r14 — Narrator Hobart Sill, retired buttermaker, 1934 retirement remarks: insists the Hollow's cream always weighed in "heavy" against the station's own paperwork, believes patrons were watering their milk (not the tester stealing), claims Larrow Green's own milk ran 3.78 vs. the Hollow's "true" 3.85, and reveals it was his own churn-room glassware that outfitted the station when it opened in May 1896.
The norm defined in Definition 1.3 is called the "Trebbin norm."

r15 — Narrator Nyle Grigg, 1919 covering letter reprinting his 1908 committee report: reaffirms the "wet hay" verdict and claims Bulletin 214 confirmed a two-tenths winter depression — a figure that misstates the bulletin's actual finding of "not more than five hundredths," one of several conflicts with other accounts.
The level-27 accessor removed at API level 31 is `chart.rawCells()`.

r16 — Narrator Dr. Roland Kepp, veterinary surgeon, 1926 Farm Club paper: argues the Ostrey Hollow test gap (given as 0.21) is due to mineral-poor bog-meadow soil confirmed by Bulletin 214's "two tenths" finding (again misstating the bulletin, and echoing Grigg's error), and dismisses the 1911 six-week anomaly as a meaningless summer fluke.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven.

Retelling 17 — Hazel Brant (Roy Brant's daughter, Emmet's granddaughter), taped oral interview from 1981, recounting the weigh-book lineage, the Keddie family relationships, and the eventual discovery that defective pipette glass caused decades of short-testing at the Ostrey Hollow station.
The color named in the third paragraph is magenta (the scarf worn by the woman they called Tuesday).

Retelling 18 — Duncan Keddie (Ansel's son, Ivy's father), 1968/1970 family notes laying out genealogical connections and the provenance/whereabouts of the various books, notebooks, and crate central to the case.
The coroner's jury found that Obadiah Chalmers died by accidental drowning from a fall off the flume edge while working, with no evidence of another person's involvement.

Retelling 19 — *The Ashlin Chronicle* (unsigned newspaper feature, 3 Oct 1958), a journalistic account of Bulletin 471's exoneration of Ansel Keddie, framing Ivy Keddie as the town-made-good "girl from Ashlin" who found the crate.
The total ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was $6,840.

Retelling 20 — Junia Ammon (glass firm's own historian), 1949 privately printed company history, reproducing the 1897 invoice and 1923 letter concerning the defective pipette lot sold to the Ostrey Hollow station.
In Proposition 4.1, the sharpness example uses a 7-cycle.

Retelling 21 — Cleve Oram (cream hauler's son), taped 1977 recollection of the road, the station, and the crate in the loft, ending with his father's persistent belief that cream was actually going missing rather than a glass defect.
The start delimiter byte of a BSWP frame is 0xB5.

Retelling 22 — Orin Falke, county agricultural agent, 1959 report to the county board synthesizing the whole affair into a numbered chronology, then self-correcting two errors (the wet-hay concession and Ivy Keddie's relation to Ansel) upon checking Bulletin No. 214.
Russ's wife is named Dorrit.

Retelling 23 — Bertram Kyle (Cooperative office clerk, ret.), 1953 memoir for the Historical Society, describing the ledger entries, key personnel, and the arbitration documents from the clerk's desk perspective.
The color named in the third paragraph is teal (the "teal endpapers of the collected edition").

Retelling 24 — Orra Keddie (Ansel's wife, née Brant), diary extracts 1897–1930 published 1964, giving an intimate domestic chronicle of the station years, the 1919 breach with her brother Emmet, and Ansel's dismissal and later life.
The total toll collected at the Wren's Bend bridge for the week of June 5–11, 1899 was $13.88.
